weeks.context:
Excel is where most BI work still happens in the real world. Even if your team uses Power BI or Tableau, you will get raw data in a spreadsheet, do quick analysis in Excel, and communicate findings in Excel before they ever reach a dashboard. Every BI analyst who thinks they are "above Excel" eventually hits a deadline where it is the fastest tool and they are slow because they never learned it properly.

This week you learn the Excel features that matter for data analysis: PivotTables, VLOOKUP/XLOOKUP, dynamic arrays (FILTER, SORT, UNIQUE), and conditional formatting. These are the building blocks for every BI task that follows.

The mindset shift: Excel is not a spreadsheet app for numbers — it is a data transformation and presentation tool. A well-structured Excel workbook with a data tab, a calculations tab, and a charts tab is a legitimate BI artefact that a business user can open and trust.

items.title: Power Query clean
items.body:
Power Query is open from yesterday. You see 3 tables on the left.

STEP 1 — Click the Orders table.

STEP 2 — Set column types.
  Click Order Date column → change type to Date.
  Click Ship Date column → Date.
  Click Sales, Profit, Discount → Decimal Number.

STEP 3 — Remove Row ID.
  Right-click Row ID column → Remove.

STEP 4 — Add Profit Margin column.
  Add Column tab → Custom Column.
  Name: Margin
  Formula: = [Profit] / [Sales]
  OK. Set the new column type to Percentage.

STEP 5 — Rename Sub-Category to Subcategory (consistency).
  Right-click → Rename.

STEP 6 — Click 'Close & Apply' (top left).
  Power BI Desktop reopens with your data loaded.

STEP 7 — Save the file.
  File → Save As → superstore.pbix → in your superstore-bi folder.

days.title: Build a date dimension table
days.summary: BI works best with a separate calendar table. Today we make one.

items.title: Create DimDate
items.body:
STEP 1 — In Power BI Desktop, Modeling tab → New table.

STEP 2 — In the formula bar, type:
      DimDate = CALENDAR(DATE(2020,1,1), DATE(2024,12,31))
  Press Enter.
  YOU SHOULD SEE: a new table called DimDate with one column 'Date'.

STEP 3 — Add columns. With DimDate selected, Modeling tab → New column.
      Year = YEAR(DimDate[Date])
  New column again:
      Month = FORMAT(DimDate[Date], "MMM")
  New column:
      Quarter = "Q" & QUARTER(DimDate[Date])

STEP 4 — Connect to Orders.
  Click the Model view (middle icon on the left sidebar).
  Drag DimDate[Date] onto Orders[Order Date].
  YOU SHOULD SEE: a line connecting them. Cardinality should be One-to-Many.

STEP 5 — Save.

days.title: Write 6 DAX measures
days.summary: DAX = the formula language of Power BI. Today: 6 measures.

items.title: DAX measures
items.body:
STEP 1 — In Power BI Desktop, click the Orders table on the right.
  Modeling tab → New measure.

STEP 2 — Type these one at a time. After each, press Enter and Modeling → New measure again:

      Total Sales = SUM(Orders[Sales])

      Total Profit = SUM(Orders[Profit])

      Profit Margin = DIVIDE([Total Profit], [Total Sales])

      Sales LY = CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(DimDate[Date]))

      YoY Growth = DIVIDE([Total Sales] - [Sales LY], [Sales LY])

      Sales YTD = TOTALYTD([Total Sales], DimDate[Date])

STEP 3 — Test in a card.
  Click the Report view (top icon on left sidebar).
  In the Visualizations pane, click the 'Card' icon.
  Drag [Total Sales] into Fields.
  YOU SHOULD SEE: $2,297,200 (or similar) in a big card. Your first DAX measure rendered.

days.title: Build the dashboard page
days.summary: Today you arrange everything into a 1-page dashboard.

items.title: Lay it out
items.body:
STEP 1 — In Report view, you have a blank canvas. Plan the layout:
  TOP (4 cards): Total Sales | Total Profit | Profit Margin | YoY Growth
  MIDDLE LEFT: line chart of Sales over time
  MIDDLE RIGHT: bar chart of Sales by Region
  BOTTOM: matrix of Subcategory + Margin
  LEFT SIDE: date slicer

STEP 2 — 4 KPI cards.
  Click Card visual. Drag Total Sales. Resize to ~200x100. Place top-left.
  Repeat for Total Profit, Profit Margin, YoY Growth — 4 cards in a row.

STEP 3 — Line chart.
  Click Line chart. Axis = DimDate[Year-Month] (or just Date). Values = Total Sales.
  Place in middle-left, sized ~500x300.

STEP 4 — Bar chart.
  Click Clustered bar chart. Axis = Region. Values = Total Sales.
  Middle-right, ~400x300.

STEP 5 — Matrix.
  Click Matrix. Rows = Subcategory. Values = Profit Margin.
  Click the dropdown next to Margin → Conditional Formatting → Background → set up:
    > 20% green, 5-20% yellow, < 5% red.
  Place at the bottom.

STEP 6 — Date slicer.
  Click Slicer. Drag DimDate[Date]. Change type to 'Between' or 'Relative date'.
  Place on the left side.

STEP 7 — Use colors consistently. Format the canvas. Add a title at the top.
  Save.

mastery_questions: VLOOKUP was, for two decades, the formula every analyst lived by — you give it a value, it searches the leftmost column of a table and returns something from a column to its right. The catch that burned everyone: VLOOKUP can only look rightward (the lookup column must sit left of what you return), and it points at the answer column by a fragile position number, so inserting a column silently breaks every formula. XLOOKUP is the modern replacement that fixes both — you hand it a lookup array and a separate return array, so it searches in any direction and does not care where the columns sit. Picture a table with ID in column C and the name you need in column A: VLOOKUP simply cannot reach left to A; XLOOKUP does it trivially. Show me one lookup that VLOOKUP cannot handle, and rewrite it in XLOOKUP.

A PivotTable is Excel's tool for collapsing thousands of raw rows into a summary without writing a single formula — you drag fields into zones and it aggregates for you. Say you have transaction rows with Date, Region, Category, Sales and Profit — one row per sale, far too many to read. To answer 'total profit by Region and Category', think in terms of the zones: Region goes into Rows, Category into Columns (or nested under Region in Rows), and Profit into Values, where Excel defaults to Sum. The mental model that matters: Rows and Columns define the groups, Values defines what gets aggregated within each group. Walk me through which field you would drop into each zone for that report, and tell me what visually changes if you put Category in Columns versus nested under Region in Rows.

A dynamic array is an Excel 365 feature where one formula can return many results that 'spill' into the cells below and beside it automatically — you write a single formula and a whole range of answers appears. FILTER is the headline example: FILTER(data, condition) returns every row matching your condition, live. Here is the distinction from a PivotTable that trips people up: a PivotTable is a static snapshot you must remember to refresh when data changes, while FILTER is a live formula that recalculates the instant the source changes — and its spilled output is a real range other formulas can build on. So FILTER is for live, formula-driven views; a PivotTable is for interactive exploration. Give me a situation where FILTER is clearly the better tool than a PivotTable, and explain what 'spill' means the moment you press Enter.

SUMIF and SUMIFS both add up numbers that meet a condition, and the whole difference is hiding in that final 'S' — it means plural conditions. SUMIF takes exactly one criterion: 'sum Sales where Region is West'. SUMIFS takes many, all of which must be true together (AND logic): 'sum Sales where Region is West AND Category is Technology'. The argument order also flips, which catches everyone — SUMIF is (range, criteria, sum_range), while SUMIFS leads with the sum_range first, then pairs of (criteria_range, criteria). For our two-condition example you would write SUMIFS(Sales, Region, "West", Category, "Technology"). Write that formula out for me, and explain why you could never express that two-condition sum with plain SUMIF.

This is a judgement question every analyst faces daily: when do you reach for a PivotTable versus a formula like SUMIFS? Think of it as exploration versus production. A PivotTable is unbeatable for exploring — drag fields around, regroup, and discover the shape of the data in seconds — but it is a manual snapshot someone has to remember to refresh. A formula-based summary (SUMIFS into a fixed layout) is the right call when you are building something that must update live, feed other calculations, or sit in a fixed template a colleague reruns every week. The rule of thumb: PivotTable to explore and answer one-off questions, formulas to build something durable and automated. Tell me, for a dashboard your manager opens every Monday expecting fresh numbers, which you would choose and why.

weeks.pre_flight:
**Download the sample dataset:**
Superstore Sales data — this is the industry-standard BI training dataset.
Download from: https://community.tableau.com/s/question/0D54T00000CWeX8SAL/sample-superstore-sales-excelxls

**Excel skills to practise this week:**

PivotTable (insert → PivotTable):
- Drag Region to Rows, Sales to Values → profit by region
- Add a slicer (PivotTable Analyze → Insert Slicer) for Category

XLOOKUP (replaces VLOOKUP):
```excel
=XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found])
```

Dynamic arrays (Excel 365/2019+):
```excel
=FILTER(A2:D100, C2:C100="West")     -- filter rows by condition
=SORT(A2:D100, 3, -1)                -- sort by column 3 descending
=UNIQUE(B2:B100)                     -- unique values from a column
```

SUMIFS:
```excel
=SUMIFS(Sales, Region, "West", Category, "Technology")
```
common_mistakes: Hardcoding values in formulas instead of referencing cells — '=SUMIFS(Sales, Region, "West")' makes the formula unmaintainable. Reference a cell that contains 'West' instead.
Not converting raw data to an Excel Table (Ctrl+T) — Tables auto-expand when you add rows, making formulas and PivotTables much more reliable.
Using merged cells — merged cells break sorting, filtering, and PivotTables. Never merge cells in a data range.
Storing data in a formatted report layout — a BI data source should be flat: one row per record, one column per attribute. Format for presentation separately.
Not using named ranges — a formula referencing 'SalesData[Sales]' is readable; one referencing 'C2:C10000' is not.
weeks.debug_help:
**PivotTable not refreshing after data change?**
Right-click the PivotTable → Refresh. Or: Data tab → Refresh All.

**XLOOKUP returning #N/A?**
```excel
-- Add a fallback value
=XLOOKUP(A2, LookupTable[ID], LookupTable[Name], "Not Found")
```

**FILTER returning a spill error (#SPILL!)?**
-- The cells below the formula are not empty. Clear them.
-- Or wrap in INDEX to return just one value:
```excel
=INDEX(FILTER(A2:D100, C2:C100="West"), 1, 1)
```

**Data mixed with text and numbers in the same column?**
-- Excel treats text-numbers differently. Use VALUE() to convert:
```excel
=SUMIFS(VALUE(C2:C100), D2:D100, "West")
```

weeks.title: Superstore BI v0.2: Drillthrough + tooltips
weeks.context:
Drillthrough is one of the most powerful features in Power BI and Tableau — it lets a user click on a data point and navigate to a detail page scoped to exactly that item. Instead of building 10 separate reports for 10 regions, you build one drillthrough page and every region gets its own contextual detail view.

Tooltips extend the base visualisation by showing additional information when a user hovers over a data point — without cluttering the main chart. Used well, they surface secondary metrics (like profit margin when hovering over a sales bar) that would otherwise need a separate chart.

This week you build these features in Power BI Desktop (free) using the Superstore dataset. The underlying skill being practised is information hierarchy: what is the primary view, what is the detail, and when should each be shown.

items.title: Plan the detail page
items.body: When a user right-clicks a region on the bar chart and chooses 'Drillthrough', what should the detail page show? List 5 visuals.

items.title: New page
items.body:
In Power BI Desktop, click + to add a new page. Rename it 'Region Detail'.
Add visuals:
  - Card: Total Sales
  - Card: Total Profit

  - Bar chart: Subcategory profit

items.title: Drillthrough field

Drag Orders[Region] into 'Drill through filters'.
An arrow appears at top-left of the page (back button) — keep it.

Go to the main page. Right-click on a Region bar → Drill through → Region Detail.
YOU SHOULD SEE: the detail page filtered to that region.

Add: Card with Total Sales, Card with Total Profit, small bar of monthly trend.

On the main page's bar chart of Subcategory, in Format → Tooltip → set 'Tooltip page' = 'Tooltip — Subcategory'.
Hover over a bar — you see your custom tooltip.

mastery_questions: These two sound alike but do opposite things, and mixing them up confuses every stakeholder you demo to. Drill-down stays on the same visual and moves through a hierarchy — you click a year in a bar chart and it expands into quarters, then months, all in that same chart. Drillthrough sends you to a different, detailed page that is automatically filtered to whatever you right-clicked — click 'West region' and you land on a fresh page showing every order in the West. So drill-down is 'zoom into the hierarchy right here', while drillthrough is 'jump to a detail page about this specific thing'. Give me one business question best answered by drill-down and one best answered by drillthrough, and explain why swapping them would frustrate the user.

The magic question with drillthrough is: how does the detail page know to show only the West region, when you never typed 'West' anywhere on it? The answer is the drillthrough filter field. When you build a drillthrough page, you drag a field (say Region) into the page's Drillthrough filter well — that tells Power BI 'this page is parameterised by Region'. Then when a user right-clicks any visual elsewhere that carries a Region context and chooses Drill through, Power BI passes that specific value into the page's filter, and every visual on the detail page silently inherits it. The detail page is essentially a template waiting to be told which value to focus on. Explain back to me what you must place in the drillthrough well for a product-detail page, and what happens if you forget to add it.

Let's build it together: you have a Sales-by-Region bar chart, and you want a user to click 'West' and see product-level detail just for the West. Three moves make it work. First, create a new page and add the visuals you want on the detail view — a table of products, their sales, maybe a chart. Second — the step beginners skip — drag Region into that page's Drillthrough filter well, which arms the page to accept a region value. Third, back on the bar chart, the user right-clicks the West bar and picks 'Drill through', and Power BI carries 'West' into the detail page's filter so every visual recomputes for West only. Walk me through those three steps in your own words, and tell me which one, if omitted, makes the whole feature silently fail.

A default tooltip is the little box that pops up when you hover a data point, showing the raw values behind it — useful but plain. A custom tooltip page is a mini-report you design yourself (charts, KPIs, formatting) and then assign to appear on hover instead of that plain box — so hovering a region's bar could surface a tiny trend line and profit figure for that region, right under the cursor. You build it as a small page sized like a tooltip, set its page type to Tooltip, and bind it to the relevant field. The point is to give context-rich insight without forcing a click or a page change. Tell me what advantage a custom tooltip page gives over the default, and one case where adding one would actually clutter rather than help.

This is really a design-judgement question about how much detail to surface, and when. Think of it as three depths of curiosity. A tooltip answers a glance — 'what is this exact value?' — instantly on hover, no commitment. A drillthrough answers a focused follow-up — 'tell me everything about this one thing I clicked' — a deliberate jump for a single entity. A separate report page answers a whole standing question a user returns to regularly. Put detail in the wrong layer and you either bury insight (too deep) or drown the glance-level view (too shallow). Give me one piece of information and argue which of the three layers it belongs in, and what breaks if you misplace it.

weeks.title: Superstore BI v0.3: Row-level security
weeks.context:
Row-level security (RLS) is what makes a BI report multi-tenant — the same report shows different data to different users based on their identity. A regional sales manager sees only their region. A product manager sees only their product category. The CEO sees everything.

Without RLS, sharing a Power BI report means sharing all the data in it. With RLS, you can publish one report to an entire organisation and each person sees only what they are authorised to see. This is not optional in enterprise BI — it is required any time data access needs to be restricted by role.

This week you implement RLS in Power BI Desktop using static roles, then learn how dynamic RLS works using USERPRINCIPALNAME() — the function that returns the logged-in user's email address and enables automatic filtering based on identity.

items.title: Model the roles
items.body:
How many roles do you need?
  - CEO: sees everything
  - WestVP: only West
  - EastVP: only East
  - CentralVP: only Central
  - SouthVP: only South

items.title: Modeling tab
items.body:
Modeling tab → Manage roles → Create.
Role: WestVP. Table: Orders. Filter: [Region] = "West"

Why is RLS enforced at the data model level, not the visual level?
What's the auditability story when a user views a report?
What's the gotcha with relationships and RLS?
mastery_questions: Row-Level Security (RLS) restricts which rows of data a user can see inside a report — same report, a different slice for each person. The two flavours differ in how the filter is decided. Static RLS hard-codes the rule into a named role: you create a 'West' role filtered to Region = West, then manually assign the West manager to it — simple, but you need one role per slice and you maintain the assignments by hand. Dynamic RLS uses a single role whose filter is computed at runtime from the logged-in user's identity, so one rule serves everyone and new users just work. Static suits a handful of fixed groups; dynamic suits many users or frequent change. Tell me, for a report shared with three department heads versus one shared with 500 sales reps, which you would pick each time and why.

Fifty regional managers, each seeing only their own region — this is the textbook case for dynamic RLS, and understanding why teaches the whole concept. With static RLS you would create fifty separate roles and manually assign each manager, then build a new role every time the company adds a region — an unmaintainable treadmill. Dynamic RLS instead stores a mapping (which user owns which region) in a table, and a single role filters the data to wherever the logged-in user's email matches that mapping — one rule, scaling to fifty or five thousand without new roles. The lesson: when the number of slices is large or changing, push the logic into data, not into hand-built roles. Walk me through the mapping table you would need and the single filter rule that makes one role serve all fifty.

USERPRINCIPALNAME() is the DAX function at the heart of dynamic RLS — it returns the identity (usually the email) of the user currently viewing the report, which is the hook you use to filter their data down to just their rows. So a dynamic rule reads something like 'show rows where this region's manager-email equals USERPRINCIPALNAME()'. The catch is testing: in Power BI Desktop you are not logged in as those fifty users, so the function would just return your own identity — which is why Desktop gives you 'View as', letting you impersonate a specific user or role to confirm the filter behaves before you publish. Explain what USERPRINCIPALNAME() returns in the live Service, and why 'View as' is the only way to trust your RLS before real users hit it.

Here is a subtle, important point: when you put an RLS filter on Orders where Region = West, does it also restrict the related Customers, Products or Returns tables? The answer is yes — but only in the direction your relationships flow. RLS filters propagate along relationship cross-filter direction exactly like any other filter in the model, so a filter on the fact table flows to a dimension only if the cross-filtering allows it, and a filter on a dimension flows to the fact table it relates to. The mistake juniors make is assuming the filter magically protects every table; if a table is not connected, or the cross-filter direction is wrong, data leaks. Explain how a filter on one table reaches another, and what you would check to be sure no related table is accidentally left unfiltered.

RLS gets defined in Power BI Desktop but enforced in the Power BI Service — and confusing where it 'happens' leads people to ship reports they believe are secure but are not. In Desktop you create the roles and write the filter rules, and you can test them with 'View as', but Desktop does not enforce RLS on you as the author — you see everything. Enforcement only kicks in once the report is published to the Service and you assign real users to those roles there; an unassigned user, or the dataset owner, may still see every row. The takeaway: defining a role is not the same as protecting data — assignment in the Service is the step that actually locks it down. Tell me the exact sequence from 'I wrote a role in Desktop' to 'a real user is safely restricted', and where the security would silently fail if you stopped early.

weeks.context:
A dashboard that doesn't refresh is a snapshot, not a BI tool. Data refresh is what makes Power BI a living reporting system — reports update automatically as the underlying data changes, without anyone manually re-uploading a file.

Power BI has two refresh paths: cloud data sources (SQL databases in Azure, BigQuery, Snowflake) refresh directly from the Service with stored credentials. On-premise data sources (a local SQL Server, an Excel file on a company network drive) require a Power BI Gateway — software installed on a machine in the corporate network that acts as a secure bridge between Power BI Service in the cloud and data sources on-premise.

This week you configure scheduled refresh in the Power BI Service and understand the gateway architecture. You also learn incremental refresh — the pattern that refreshes only new/changed data instead of reloading the entire dataset, which is critical for large data sources.

What's the difference between Import mode and DirectQuery?
mastery_questions: Import and DirectQuery are the two ways Power BI gets at your data, and the choice shapes everything about performance and freshness. Import mode pulls a copy of the data into Power BI's own in-memory engine — blisteringly fast to slice and dice, but the data is a snapshot frozen at the last refresh, so you must schedule refreshes to keep it current. DirectQuery leaves the data in the source and sends a live query every time someone interacts — always current, no refresh needed, but every click waits on the source database, so it is slower and leans entirely on that database's health. Import trades freshness for speed; DirectQuery trades speed for freshness. Tell me which you would choose for a daily executive dashboard over a fairly static dataset, versus a report that must reflect live inventory to the second, and explain the refresh implication of each.

This question is really about a trust-and-networking problem: the Power BI Service lives in the cloud, but the SQL Server sits inside a company's private network behind a firewall — so how does the cloud reach data it is not allowed to connect to directly? The answer is the on-premises data gateway: a small piece of software installed on a machine inside the corporate network that acts as a secure broker. When the Service needs to refresh, it sends the request to the gateway over an encrypted outbound channel the firewall permits, the gateway runs the query against the local SQL Server, and passes the results back up — the database is never directly exposed to the internet. Walk me through that round trip from 'scheduled refresh starts in the cloud' to 'rows arrive', and explain why the gateway lives inside the network rather than in the cloud.

Incremental refresh is the technique that keeps large datasets from becoming unrefreshable. Without it, every scheduled refresh reloads the entire table — fine for 10,000 rows, catastrophic for 500 million, where a full reload might take hours or simply fail. Incremental refresh splits the data by date into partitions and only reloads the recent window that actually changes (say, the last 10 days), leaving the historical partitions untouched. To set it up you define two parameters, RangeStart and RangeEnd, that Power BI uses to slice the table, then a policy stating how much history to keep and how much recent data to refresh. Explain why reloading only the recent partitions is so much cheaper, and what the RangeStart and RangeEnd parameters are actually doing under the hood.

A scheduled refresh that fails at 6am every day is a classic ops puzzle, and a good analyst reasons from the refresh pipeline rather than guessing. Three usual suspects, each a different link in the chain: first, credentials — a password or token the gateway uses to reach the source expired, so authentication fails; second, the gateway or source itself — the machine hosting the gateway was off, or the source database was down for maintenance at that hour; third, the data — a schema change such as a renamed column, or a query timeout because the morning data volume spiked, broke the load. The discipline is mapping a symptom to the stage that produces it. Give me your three most likely causes for this exact 6am failure, and for one of them tell me what log or error message would confirm it.

People say 'refresh the report' loosely, but Power BI has two distinct operations, and the difference matters for troubleshooting. A dataset refresh re-pulls the underlying data from the source into the model — this is the heavy, scheduled operation that actually updates the numbers. A report refresh just re-renders the visuals against the data already in the model — it is what happens when you hit refresh in the browser to redraw the charts, and it shows new data only if the dataset behind it was refreshed first. So a stakeholder complaining 'I refreshed but the numbers are old' almost always refreshed the report, not the dataset. Explain the two clearly, and tell me which one a scheduled 6am job is doing and which one a user clicking refresh in their browser is doing.

weeks.title: Power BI Fundamentals
weeks.context:
You have been using Power BI to build Superstore reports for 4 weeks. This week you close the gaps — learning the fundamentals you may have skipped over while focused on features. The fundamentals that most analysts skip and then spend years trying to fix: data modelling, DAX basics, and the semantic layer.

Power BI's architecture has three layers: data (Power Query — Extract, Transform, Load), model (relationships, hierarchies, measures), and report (visuals, interactions). Most analysts work only in the report layer and wonder why their numbers are wrong. Your numbers are wrong because of mistakes in the model layer.

DAX (Data Analysis Expressions) is the formula language for measures. Measures are not calculated columns — a measure is a formula that responds to filter context. Understanding filter context is the single most important concept in Power BI. Every wrong number you see in a report is a filter context problem.

mastery_questions: This is the single most important distinction in Power BI, and getting it wrong wrecks both performance and correctness. A calculated column is computed once, row by row, when the data refreshes, and the result is stored in the table — it takes up memory and its value is fixed regardless of how the user later slices the report. A measure is computed on the fly, at the moment a visual asks for it, and it respects whatever filters the user has applied — it stores nothing and recalculates constantly. The rule: use a calculated column when you need a per-row value to slice or group by (a category label, a flag); use a measure for any aggregation that should react to filters (sums, ratios, running totals). Give me one thing that must be a calculated column and one that must be a measure, and explain what goes wrong if you swap them.

Filter context is the idea that makes DAX click — and until it does, measures feel like magic. Filter context is the set of filters in force at the exact moment a measure is evaluated: the slicers the user picked, the row and column a value sits in, the page-level filters. So when a slicer is set to 'West Region', every measure recalculates as if only West rows exist — that filter is silently applied before your expression runs. CALCULATE() is the one function that can deliberately change that context — it evaluates its expression under a modified set of filters you specify. Walk me through what the filter context is for a single cell in a matrix of Sales by Region and Year, and then explain what CALCULATE() does to that context when you wrap it.

A star schema is a data model with one central fact table (the events — your sales rows) surrounded by dimension tables (the descriptive lookups — Date, Product, Customer, Region), each joined to the fact by a key, forming a star shape. Power BI's engine is built and optimised for exactly this shape, which is why it is the strong recommendation. The alternative — a single flat table where every sale carries its full product name, customer address and region details repeated on every row — causes real problems: it bloats memory by repeating text millions of times, makes relationships and time-intelligence awkward, and slows the engine that expects dimensions to filter facts. Explain why a flat table repeats so much data, and what specifically the star schema gives the engine that a flat table denies it.

CALCULATE() is the most powerful function in DAX because it can override the filters a user has set, rather than just obeying them. It takes an expression plus one or more filter arguments, evaluates the expression, but first modifies the filter context with those arguments. The classic example: you want a measure that always shows Technology sales no matter which category the user clicks in a slicer. You write CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), Sales[Category] = "Technology") — the filter argument forces Category to Technology, replacing whatever the slicer said. That ability to ignore or replace user filters is what unlocks ratios-to-total, year-over-year, and fixed baselines. Write that Technology measure for me, and explain precisely what CALCULATE does to the slicer's filter when the user has picked 'Furniture'.

A dedicated Date table feels like bureaucracy until you need time intelligence, and then it becomes non-negotiable. The date column buried in your fact table only contains the dates on which something actually happened — so if no sale occurred on a given day, that day does not exist, and any 'same period last year' or 'running total' calculation will have gaps and lie to you. A dedicated Date table is a complete, continuous calendar (every day in the range, with year, quarter, month, weekday columns) that DAX time-intelligence functions like SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR rely on to navigate time correctly. It is also the clean place to build a fiscal calendar or holiday flags. Explain what breaks in a year-over-year measure when you lean on the fact table's date column instead of a proper Date table.

**Power BI data model basics:**

**Create a proper Date table in DAX:**
```dax
DateTable =
ADDCOLUMNS(
    CALENDAR(DATE(2020,1,1), DATE(2025,12,31)),
    "Year", YEAR([Date]),
    "Month", MONTH([Date]),
    "MonthName", FORMAT([Date], "MMMM"),
    "Quarter", "Q" & QUARTER([Date]),
    "WeekNum", WEEKNUM([Date])
)
```

**Core DAX measures:**
```dax
Total Sales = SUM(Orders[Sales])
Total Profit = SUM(Orders[Profit])
Profit Margin = DIVIDE([Total Profit], [Total Sales], 0)
YTD Sales = TOTALYTD([Total Sales], DateTable[Date])
PY Sales = CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(DateTable[Date]))
Sales Growth = DIVIDE([Total Sales] - [PY Sales], [PY Sales], 0)
```
common_mistakes: Using calculated columns instead of measures for aggregations — calculated columns compute once at load time and are stored in memory. Measures compute dynamically based on filter context. Use measures for any aggregation.

Not marking the Date table as a Date table — Power BI won't use time intelligence functions (TOTALYTD, SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR) correctly unless you mark the table: Table tools → Mark as date table.
Using SUM instead of SUMX when you need row-by-row calculation — SUM adds a column; SUMX evaluates a row expression and then sums the results.
Not using DIVIDE() instead of / for division — DIVIDE(numerator, denominator, 0) handles division by zero gracefully. The / operator returns an error.

weeks.context:
Advanced DAX is the difference between a BI analyst who builds reports and one who builds data products. The features this week — variables, iterator functions, and advanced CALCULATE patterns — are what you need to express complex business logic that no visual configuration can handle.

Variables in DAX (VAR / RETURN) are not just a code style preference — they change evaluation. A variable captures the current filter context at the point it is declared, which prevents a common class of DAX bugs where the context changes unexpectedly inside a complex expression.

Iterator functions (SUMX, AVERAGEX, MAXX, RANKX) evaluate an expression row by row and then aggregate. They are essential when your calculation requires a per-row computation before summing — like calculating profit margin per order and then averaging those margins, rather than dividing total profit by total sales.

mastery_questions: SUM and SUMX look similar but think differently, and the gap shows up the moment your calculation needs to happen row by row. SUM(Sales[Amount]) adds an existing column — it assumes the number you want is already sitting there. SUMX is an iterator: it walks the table row by row, evaluates an expression for each row, and then totals the results. The trap is a calculation like total revenue when you only have Quantity and UnitPrice in separate columns — SUM cannot multiply them per row, so SUM(Quantity) times SUM(UnitPrice) gives a nonsense number (total quantity times total price). SUMX(Sales, Sales[Quantity] * Sales[UnitPrice]) does the multiplication on each row first, then sums — the correct answer. Show me a case where SUM gives the wrong total and SUMX fixes it, and explain exactly why the SUM version is wrong.

VAR is how you store a value mid-calculation in DAX, and the subtle, crucial fact is when that value gets locked in. A VAR is evaluated once, at the point it is declared, in the filter context that exists right then — and the result is frozen for the rest of the expression, even if you reference it later inside a CALCULATE that changes the context. This is exactly why a VAR can give a different answer than pasting the same expression inline twice: the inline version re-evaluates under whatever context surrounds it each time, while the VAR captured its value early and held it. That property is a feature — it lets you grab 'this year's total' before you shift context to last year. Explain why a VAR declared before a CALCULATE keeps its original value, and give me one bug this behaviour helps you avoid.

Ranking within a group is a rite of passage in DAX, and the key insight is controlling what 'within' means. You do not want each product ranked against all products globally; you want it ranked only against the others in its own category. RANKX is the tool, but the trick is the table you hand it: you must give RANKX the set of products in the current category, not the whole product table, so the ranking resets per category. A common pattern uses RANKX over a table built with ALLEXCEPT(Products, Products[Category]) so it removes every filter except the category, ranking each product among its category peers. Sketch the measure for me, and explain what would happen to the ranking if you passed RANKX the full product table with ALL() instead.

SWITCH() is DAX's clean alternative to deeply nested IF statements — it takes a value and a list of cases, returning the result for whichever case matches. The genuinely clever pattern is dynamic measure selection: you create a small disconnected table (one not joined to anything) listing measure names like 'Sales', 'Profit', 'Margin', put it in a slicer, and write one measure that uses SWITCH on the user's selection to decide which calculation to actually return. Now a single slicer lets the user reshape the visual to show whichever metric they want, without you building three separate charts. Walk me through how the disconnected table's selected value flows into SWITCH, and why the table must be disconnected for this to work.

These three functions all remove filters, but each removes a different amount, and choosing wrong gives subtly wrong totals. ALL() removes every filter from a table or column — you use it when you need the grand total ignoring all slicers, like the denominator in a 'percent of total' measure. ALLEXCEPT() removes all filters except the ones you name — perfect when you want to clear everything but keep, say, the Category filter so you can compute a percent-within-category. REMOVEFILTERS() is the modern, clearer-named equivalent of ALL() used inside CALCULATE to strip specific filters. The skill is knowing how much context to clear for the ratio you are building. Give me a use case for each, and tell me what a percent-of-total measure returns if you accidentally use ALLEXCEPT where you needed ALL.

Variables:
```dax
Profit Margin Safe =
VAR TotalSales = [Total Sales]
VAR TotalProfit = [Total Profit]
RETURN

```

RANKX (rank products by sales):
```dax
Product Sales Rank =
RANKX(
    ALL(Products[ProductName]),
    [Total Sales],
    ,
    DESC,
    Dense
)
```

SUMX (row-by-row profit margin then sum):
```dax
Avg Order Margin =
AVERAGEX(
    Orders,
    DIVIDE(Orders[Profit], Orders[Sales], 0)
)
```

Top N with TOPN:
```dax
Top 5 Products Sales =
CALCULATE(
    [Total Sales],
    TOPN(5, ALL(Products[ProductName]), [Total Sales])
)
```

```dax
Selected Measure =
VAR SelectedValue = SELECTEDVALUE(MeasureSelector[Measure])
RETURN
    SWITCH(
        SelectedValue,
        "Sales", [Total Sales],
        "Profit", [Total Profit],
        "Margin", [Profit Margin],
        [Total Sales]
    )
```

Using TOPN for a table but forgetting it returns a table, not a scalar — wrap it in CALCULATE or use SUMX over it.

weeks.title: SQL for BI Reporting
weeks.context:
SQL is the lingua franca of data. Every BI tool — Power BI, Tableau, Looker, Metabase — eventually pushes a SQL query to a database. A BI analyst who cannot write SQL is dependent on an engineer to get data. A BI analyst who can write SQL gets data themselves and builds faster.

This week you learn the SQL patterns that appear constantly in BI work: aggregations with GROUP BY, filtering with WHERE and HAVING, joining multiple tables, window functions (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, LEAD, SUM OVER), and CTEs (Common Table Expressions) for readable complex queries.

Window functions are the most powerful SQL feature for BI — they let you compute things like running totals, rank within a group, and period-over-period comparisons at the SQL level, before the data even reaches your BI tool.

mastery_questions: WHERE and HAVING both filter rows, but they act at different moments in the query, and that timing is the whole point. WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping happens — it decides which raw rows even enter the calculation. HAVING filters after a GROUP BY has aggregated the rows — it decides which groups survive based on their aggregated values. So you cannot use WHERE to say 'only regions whose total sales exceed 100,000', because that total does not exist until after grouping — that is a HAVING job; but you can use WHERE to say 'only orders from 2024' before grouping. A query using both reads: WHERE filters the year, GROUP BY rolls up by region, HAVING keeps only the big-selling regions. Write me that query, and explain why moving the HAVING condition into WHERE would be a syntax or logic error.

Window functions are the feature that turns SQL from a grouping tool into an analytical one, and the unlock is this: unlike GROUP BY, they let you compute across a set of rows while still keeping every individual row. PARTITION BY is what defines that set — it slices the data into groups for the calculation, but does not collapse them. Picture ranking salespeople within each region: GROUP BY region would crush each region into one summary row and lose the individuals, but a window function with PARTITION BY region computes the rank inside each region while every salesperson's row stays visible. So GROUP BY answers 'one number per group'; PARTITION BY answers 'a per-row number computed within each group'. Explain that difference with your own example, and tell me what PARTITION BY is doing that GROUP BY cannot.

Ranking each product within its category is the classic window-function exercise, so let's reason through the tools. You want a rank that restarts for every category, and the row-by-row detail preserved — that is exactly what RANK() or ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY sales DESC) gives you: PARTITION BY category resets the numbering per category, ORDER BY sales DESC ranks the best seller as 1. The piece beginners forget is the ORDER BY inside the OVER clause — without it, 'rank' has no meaning because the window does not know what to rank by. Write the query for me, and tell me the difference you would see in the output between RANK() and ROW_NUMBER() when two products in a category have identical sales.

A CTE (Common Table Expression) is a named, temporary result set defined with WITH at the top of your query, which you then reference by name below as if it were a table. Its value is readability and maintenance: a deeply nested subquery forces the reader to mentally unwrap it from the inside out, while a CTE lets you name each logical step ('first, monthly_totals; then, ranked_months') and read top to bottom like a story. It also lets you reference the same intermediate result twice without repeating it. Take a query with a subquery nested inside another, rewrite it as one or two CTEs, and explain to me which is easier for the next analyst to debug at 2am, and why.

Month-over-month growth is a rite-of-passage SQL query because it forces you to compare a row to the row before it — something SQL does not do naturally without help. The modern approach uses the LAG() window function: after aggregating sales by month, LAG(monthly_sales) OVER (ORDER BY month) fetches the previous month's value onto the current row, and then growth is simply (this_month minus last_month) divided by last_month. The insight is that LAG turns a 'compare to the prior period' problem into a single row-level subtraction. Write me that query in two stages — aggregate to monthly totals, then apply LAG for the growth percentage — and tell me what LAG returns for the very first month and how you would handle it.

**Core SQL patterns for BI:**
```sql
-- Aggregation with GROUP BY
SELECT region, SUM(sales) as total_sales, AVG(profit) as avg_profit
FROM orders
GROUP BY region
ORDER BY total_sales DESC;

-- HAVING (filter on aggregation)
SELECT category, SUM(sales) as total_sales
FROM orders
GROUP BY category
HAVING SUM(sales) > 100000;

-- Window function: running total
SELECT order_date, sales,
       SUM(sales) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) as running_total
FROM orders;

-- Window function: rank within partition
SELECT product_name, category, sales,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY sales DESC) as rank_in_category
FROM orders;

-- CTE for readability
WITH regional_totals AS (
    SELECT region, SUM(sales) as total_sales
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY region
),
grand_total AS (
    SELECT SUM(sales) as total FROM orders
)
SELECT r.region, r.total_sales,
       ROUND(r.total_sales / g.total * 100, 2) as pct_of_total
FROM regional_totals r, grand_total g
ORDER BY r.total_sales DESC;
```
common_mistakes: Using WHERE to filter on aggregated values — WHERE runs before aggregation. Use HAVING to filter after GROUP BY.
SELECT * in production queries — always specify the columns you need. SELECT * pulls unnecessary data and breaks when schema changes.
Not aliasing calculated columns — 'SUM(sales)' becomes 'sum(sales)' in some databases. Always alias: 'SUM(sales) AS total_sales'.
Joining on non-indexed columns — JOINs on unindexed columns are slow on large tables. Check that your JOIN keys are indexed.
Using DISTINCT instead of GROUP BY to remove duplicates — DISTINCT is coarser. GROUP BY lets you aggregate while deduplicating.

weeks.title: Data Modelling and Warehouse Concepts
weeks.context:
Data warehousing is the backend of BI. When a company scales beyond Excel and Power BI files, they build a data warehouse — a centralised repository of integrated, historical data designed for analysis rather than transactions.

The key concepts: OLTP vs OLAP (transactional databases optimised for writes vs analytical databases optimised for reads), dimensional modelling (star and snowflake schemas), slowly changing dimensions (how to handle data that changes over time, like a customer's address), and fact table granularity (what exactly one row represents).

Modern data warehouses (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, Databricks) have largely replaced traditional on-premise warehouses. They are columnar, massively parallel, and can query petabytes in seconds. Understanding how they differ from row-based databases explains why your SQL performance patterns are different.

mastery_questions: OLTP and OLAP are two database worlds optimised for opposite jobs, and confusing them is why some reports crawl. OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) powers the live application — many tiny, fast reads and writes, like 'insert this order' or 'update this customer' — and is structured (highly normalised) to make those single-row operations safe and quick. OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) powers analytics — a few enormous queries that scan and aggregate millions of rows, like 'total sales by region by month for three years' — and is structured (star schemas, columnar storage) to make those sweeping aggregations fast. A query like that three-year roll-up flies on OLAP but crawls on OLTP, because OLTP was never built to scan everything. Give me one specific query that is fast on OLAP and slow on OLTP, and explain what about each design causes the difference.

The grain of a fact table is the precise definition of what one row represents — 'one row per order line item', or 'one row per daily sales total per store'. It sounds like a triviality, but defining grain is the very first step in dimensional modelling because every other decision flows from it: which dimensions can attach, what you can and cannot aggregate, and whether your numbers even mean what you think. Get it wrong — mixing one-row-per-order with one-row-per-line-item in the same table — and your totals double-count or your dimensions do not line up. The discipline is to state the grain in one sentence before you build anything. Tell me the grain you would choose for a retail sales fact table, and explain one analysis that becomes impossible if your grain is too coarse.

SCD Type 2 (Slowly Changing Dimension, Type 2) is how a data warehouse remembers history when an attribute changes — and the example makes it concrete. Say a customer moves from London to Paris. A naive design just overwrites 'London' with 'Paris', and now every past order they placed appears to have happened while they lived in Paris — history is corrupted. SCD Type 2 instead keeps the old row, marks it expired with an end-date, and inserts a new row for Paris with a fresh start-date and a new surrogate key — so orders placed before the move stay linked to the London row, and later orders link to Paris. The truth of 'where did they live when they ordered' is preserved. Walk me through the rows before and after the move, and explain why the surrogate key (not the customer ID) is what makes this work.

A degenerate dimension is a dimension attribute that lives right inside the fact table instead of in its own dimension table — typically a transactional identifier like an order number or invoice number. It is called 'degenerate' because it has no other descriptive attributes worth putting in a separate table; the number is meaningful on its own (for grouping line items of the same order, or tracing back to the source system) but it would be silly to build a whole Order dimension table just to hold an order ID and nothing else. In the Superstore dataset, the Order ID is the classic example — you keep it on the fact row to group line items, without a separate table. Tell me which field in Superstore you would treat as a degenerate dimension, and why building a full dimension table for it would be pointless.

Star versus snowflake is a normalisation trade-off, and Power BI has a clear preference for a performance reason. A star schema keeps each dimension as a single flat table (Product holds category and sub-category right in it). A snowflake normalises those dimensions into chains of smaller tables (Product links to a separate Category table, which links to a Department table). Snowflake saves a little storage and feels 'cleaner' to a database purist, but it forces Power BI's engine to traverse more relationships for every query, which slows filtering and complicates DAX. The engine is tuned for the short, direct fact-to-dimension hops of a star. Explain the DAX and performance cost of the extra hops in a snowflake, and when, if ever, the snowflake is still worth it.

**Dimensional modelling concepts to understand:**

Fact table:
- Contains measurable, numeric data (sales amount, quantity, profit)
- Each row = one business event at a specific grain (one order line item)
- Has foreign keys to dimension tables

Dimension table:
- Contains descriptive attributes (product name, category, customer name, city)
- Changes rarely (or uses SCD to track changes)
- Has a surrogate key (auto-incremented ID)

Star schema vs Snowflake:
- Star: dimensions are flat (one table each)
- Snowflake: dimensions are normalised into sub-dimensions (Category → Sub-category split into separate tables)
- Power BI prefers star schema for performance

Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD):
- Type 1: Overwrite old value (lose history)
- Type 2: Add new row with effective dates (keep full history)
- Type 3: Add new column for old/new value (limited history)

**Free tool: dbt Core (data transformation framework):**
```bash
pip install dbt-postgres
dbt init myproject
```
common_mistakes: Putting too much in the fact table — facts contain measures and foreign keys only. Descriptive attributes belong in dimensions.
Not defining grain before building — if your fact table has one row per order sometimes and one row per order line item other times, aggregations are wrong.
Using SCD Type 1 for dimensions where history matters — overwriting a customer's region when they move makes historical regional analysis impossible.
Building a snowflake schema in Power BI — normalising dimensions into sub-tables requires extra JOINs and slows DAX filter propagation. Denormalise into flat dimensions instead.
Not creating surrogate keys — using natural business keys (like product codes) as dimension keys makes it harder to handle SCD and source system changes.

weeks.title: Business Statistics for BI
weeks.context:
BI without statistics is opinion dressed as data. Business statistics gives you the tools to separate signal from noise, quantify uncertainty, and make claims about data that can be defended when challenged.

The statistics that BI analysts actually use daily: descriptive statistics (mean, median, standard deviation, percentiles), distributions (understanding what normal looks like so you can spot anomalies), correlation (does variable A move with variable B?), and regression (can I predict Y from X?).

The most important skill this week is statistical intuition — knowing when a trend is real versus random noise, when a correlation is meaningful versus coincidental, and when your sample size is too small to make a claim. These are the moments that determine whether a BI analyst is credible or not.

Distributions: normal, skewed, bimodal — and what they imply about the data
Correlation and causation: Pearson r, Spearman r, interpreting r-values
Outlier detection: IQR method, z-scores, and business impact of outliers
Intro to probability: conditional probability, Bayes intuition for business decisions

mastery_questions: Mean and median both try to capture 'the typical value', but they react very differently to extremes, and knowing which to trust is what separates an analyst from a calculator. The mean adds everything up and divides by the count, so every value pulls on it — including one giant outlier. The median is the middle value when you line the data up in order, so it ignores how extreme the extremes are. Picture salaries on a team where everyone earns around 50k except a founder on 5 million: the mean salary looks like several hundred thousand (a number nobody actually earns), while the median stays near 50k — the honest 'typical' figure. For skewed business data like income, deal size, or page-load times, the median usually tells the truer story. Give me a real business metric where reporting the mean would actively mislead a manager, and explain what the median reveals instead.

Standard deviation, in plain English for a manager, is a measure of how spread out your numbers are around their average — a small one means days cluster tightly near normal, a large one means they swing wildly. The way I would explain it: 'on average we sell about 500 units a day, give or take 50' — that 'give or take' is essentially the standard deviation. Its real power for you is anomaly detection: once you know normal daily sales sit within, say, one or two standard deviations of the average, a day that lands three standard deviations out is statistically unusual and worth investigating — a spike or a data error, not routine noise. That turns 'this feels high' into a defensible threshold. Explain standard deviation to a non-technical manager in one sentence, then describe how you would use it to flag an abnormal sales day.

'Sales are up 15% this month' is the kind of statement that sounds like a win but might just be noise, and your job is to tell the difference before anyone celebrates. The question is whether 15% is a real shift or normal month-to-month variation, and you answer it with context: how much do months typically bounce around (the historical standard deviation of monthly change)? A 15% rise means little if months routinely swing plus or minus 20% — it is within the noise. But if months usually move only 3%, then 15% is a genuine signal worth explaining. You can frame this with a control-chart mindset or a significance test against historical variation. Walk me through how you would decide whether this 15% is signal or noise, and what data about past months you would pull first.

Correlation means two things move together; causation means one actually drives the other — and treating the first as the second is the most expensive mistake in analytics. The classic trap is a lurking third variable: ice-cream sales and drowning deaths rise together, not because ice cream causes drowning, but because hot weather drives both. In business it bites just as hard — say you find stores with more staff have higher sales and conclude 'hire more staff to boost sales', when really high-traffic locations were given both more staff and more customers; the staffing did not cause the sales. Before you recommend an action based on a correlation, you have to ask what else could explain it. Give me a real business correlation that would mislead a decision-maker, name the hidden variable, and explain the wrong action it could trigger.

A p-value answers one narrow question: if there were truly no real effect, how likely is it that you would see a result at least this extreme just by chance? A small p-value means 'pure luck is an unlikely explanation', which is why we lean toward believing the effect is real. So p = 0.03 means there is about a 3% chance of seeing this result if the variants were actually identical — below the conventional 0.05 line, so you would typically call it statistically significant and lean toward shipping the variant. But significance is not the same as importance: a tiny, significant effect can still be commercially worthless, and p-values say nothing about effect size. Tell me what p = 0.03 lets you conclude, what it does not tell you, and what else you would check before acting on it.

**Statistics in Python — hands-on:**
```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv('superstore.csv')

# Descriptive statistics
print(df['Sales'].describe())
print(f"Median: {df['Sales'].median():.2f}")
print(f"Std Dev: {df['Sales'].std():.2f}")
print(f"90th percentile: {df['Sales'].quantile(0.9):.2f}")

# Correlation
corr = df[['Sales', 'Profit', 'Discount', 'Quantity']].corr()
print(corr)

# Distribution check
from scipy.stats import normaltest
stat, p = normaltest(df['Sales'])
print(f"Normal test p-value: {p:.4f}")
# p < 0.05 = not normally distributed

# Simple linear regression
from scipy.stats import linregress
slope, intercept, r, p, se = linregress(df['Sales'], df['Profit'])
print(f"R-squared: {r**2:.4f}, Slope: {slope:.4f}")
```
common_mistakes: Using mean when data is skewed — revenue data is almost always right-skewed (a few huge deals inflate the mean). Median revenue is more representative of the typical deal.
Claiming causation from correlation — two metrics moving together in a dashboard does not mean one causes the other. Always ask: what else changed at the same time?
Ignoring sample size when comparing percentages — '100% success rate' means nothing if it is based on 3 observations.
Not visualising the distribution before reporting the average — always plot a histogram. You may have outliers that are distorting the summary statistics.
Reporting too many decimal places — reporting 'conversion rate: 3.847612%' implies false precision. Round to 2 significant figures: 3.8%.

weeks.title: A/B Testing and Hypothesis Testing
weeks.context:
A/B testing is how data-driven companies make product decisions. Instead of debating which version of a feature is better, you run both versions simultaneously, collect data, and let statistics decide. A BI analyst's job in an A/B test: design the experiment correctly, analyse the results without bias, and communicate findings clearly.

The most common A/B testing mistakes are not statistical — they are design mistakes: running the test too short, stopping when you first see significance, testing too many variants simultaneously, and not defining the primary metric before the test starts. These mistakes produce false positives that lead companies to ship worse products.

This week you learn the statistics of A/B testing (two-sample tests, power analysis, sample size calculation) and how to run and analyse experiments using Python. You also learn the business side: how to communicate results to stakeholders who don't understand p-values.

mastery_questions: Type I and Type II errors are the two ways a hypothesis test can fool you, and naming them is less useful than feeling their cost. A Type I error (false positive) is concluding there is an effect when there is not — in an A/B test, declaring the new button a winner and shipping it, when really it does nothing. A Type II error (false negative) is missing a real effect — killing a genuinely better variant because the test did not reach significance. Which hurts more depends entirely on the cost of the action: if shipping the change is cheap and reversible, a Type I error is survivable; if shipping it means a costly engineering commitment or a risk to revenue, a false positive is the expensive one. The skill is reasoning about consequences, not just probabilities. For a checkout-flow A/B test, tell me which error you would fear more and why.

Statistical power is the probability that your test will actually detect a real effect when one exists — and ignoring it is why so many A/B tests are quietly worthless. If your sample is too small, even a genuinely better variant can fail to reach significance, and you wrongly conclude 'no difference' (a Type II error). That is why you calculate the required sample size before you run the test, not after: you decide up front how big an effect you care about detecting, how much power you want (usually 80%), and the math tells you how many users you need. Running first and checking later means you might burn weeks of traffic on a test that never had a chance of proving anything. Explain why a small sample can hide a real effect, and what three things you must decide before computing the sample size.

'Peeking' is the tempting habit of watching an A/B test's results as they come in and stopping the moment you first see p < 0.05 — and it quietly destroys the validity of your test. Here is why: p-values fluctuate as data accumulates, and even with two identical variants, the running p-value will randomly dip below 0.05 at some point just by chance. If you stop the instant you see that dip, you are cherry-picking the one moment the noise looked like signal, so your real false-positive rate is far higher than the 5% you think you have. The fix is to fix the sample size and the end date in advance and only judge at the finish line (or use methods designed for continuous monitoring). Explain why repeatedly peeking inflates false positives, and what discipline prevents it.

p = 0.03 and a manager who wants to ship immediately is a real scenario where your value is slowing the room down with the right questions, not just reporting the number. Significance alone is not enough to ship, so before you recommend it you need: the effect size (a significant 0.1% lift might not be worth the engineering cost), the sample size and whether the test ran its planned duration (did someone peek and stop early?), whether the result is stable across key segments (is it a real lift or driven by one weird cohort?), and any guardrail metrics that might have gotten worse while the headline metric improved. The point: a green p-value can still hide a bad decision. List the additional information you would gather before endorsing the ship, and explain what a good headline number could be hiding.

A one-tailed test asks whether an effect goes in one specific direction ('is the new design better?'), while a two-tailed test asks whether there is a difference in either direction ('is the new design different — better or worse?'). The two-tailed test is the safer default because it does not assume you know which way things will move, and it is harder to pass, which keeps you honest. A one-tailed test concentrates all your statistical 'budget' on one direction, making it easier to reach significance — which is exactly why it is so often misused to manufacture a positive result. You would only justify one-tailed when a worse outcome is genuinely irrelevant to your decision. Tell me a business situation where a one-tailed test is legitimately appropriate, and why using it just to get a smaller p-value is cheating.

**A/B testing in Python:**
```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# Simulate an A/B test
np.random.seed(42)
control_conversions = np.random.binomial(1, 0.10, 1000)   # 10% base rate
variant_conversions = np.random.binomial(1, 0.115, 1000)  # 15% lift

# Two-proportion z-test
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportions_ztest
count = np.array([variant_conversions.sum(), control_conversions.sum()])
nobs = np.array([len(variant_conversions), len(control_conversions)])
stat, pval = proportions_ztest(count, nobs)
print(f"Conversion A: {control_conversions.mean():.3f}")
print(f"Conversion B: {variant_conversions.mean():.3f}")
print(f"p-value: {pval:.4f}")
print(f"Result: {'Significant' if pval < 0.05 else 'Not significant'}")
```

**Sample size calculation:**
```python
from statsmodels.stats.power import NormalIndPower
analysis = NormalIndPower()
# How many users needed to detect a 15% lift with 80% power at 5% significance?
baseline = 0.10
effect_size = 0.015 / (baseline * (1 - baseline)) ** 0.5
n = analysis.solve_power(effect_size=effect_size, power=0.8, alpha=0.05)
print(f"Required sample size per variant: {int(n)}")
```
common_mistakes: Not defining the primary metric before the test starts — testing multiple metrics and reporting whichever is significant is called p-hacking. Define one primary metric in advance.
Running the test until it is significant — this is 'peeking'. The false positive rate increases every time you check. Define a sample size upfront and wait until you reach it.
Ignoring practical significance — p = 0.001 but the lift is 0.01%? Not worth shipping. Always report effect size alongside p-value.
Not checking for novelty effects — a new feature often gets higher engagement simply because it is new. Run tests long enough to see past novelty (at least 2 weeks for consumer products).
Not segmenting results — an overall non-significant result can mask a strong positive effect in a specific segment. Always analyse key segments.

weeks.title: KPIs, Metrics Design, and Data Storytelling
weeks.context:
A KPI (Key Performance Indicator) is a metric that measures progress toward a specific business objective. Most companies have too many KPIs, and most of them are vanity metrics — numbers that look good but don't tell you whether the business is healthy or how to improve it.

Good metrics have three properties: they are actionable (someone can change their behaviour based on them), they are comparable (you can tell if this week's number is good or bad by comparing to something), and they are understandable (the person being measured understands how the number is calculated).

Data storytelling is the practice of presenting data in a narrative that leads to a decision. The best BI analysts don't just produce charts — they answer "so what?" and "now what?". This week you learn both: how to design metrics that matter, and how to present them in a way that drives action.

mastery_questions: Metric, KPI, and North Star metric are three nested levels of importance, and using the words loosely makes a strategy conversation mushy. A metric is any number you can measure — page views, signups, email opens; there are thousands. A KPI (Key Performance Indicator) is the small subset of metrics you have decided actually indicate success against a goal — the ones you put on the dashboard and hold people to. A North Star metric is the single number that best captures the core value your product delivers and that the whole company rallies behind — for a SaaS company, perhaps 'weekly active teams' or 'monthly recurring revenue'. The hierarchy is: many metrics, few KPIs, one North Star. Give me an example of each for a SaaS business, and explain why elevating the wrong metric to North Star could steer the whole company astray.

A vanity metric is a number that looks impressive and reliably goes up, but does not inform a decision or tie to real value — it flatters you without guiding you. The test is simple: 'if this number doubled, would I know what to do differently?' If not, it is vanity. Total registered users is the classic one — it only ever grows and ignores whether anyone still uses the product; a better metric is active users, which can fall and force action. Total page views flatters a content site but says nothing about engagement; time-on-task or conversion is more honest. Cumulative downloads of an app looks great but hides that most users churned; retention rate tells the truth. Give me three vanity metrics, and for each one name the actionable metric you would track instead and why it drives a decision.

Leading and lagging indicators differ in timing: a lagging indicator measures an outcome that has already happened, while a leading indicator measures something earlier that predicts that outcome — so you can still influence it. Revenue is the archetypal lagging indicator: by the time it moves, the causes are months behind you and there is nothing left to adjust. A leading indicator for that same revenue might be number of qualified demos booked this week — it moves first, and a dip warns you of a revenue shortfall in time to react. The art is finding leading indicators that genuinely predict the lagging ones you care about, rather than just correlate by accident. Give me a lagging indicator for a business you know and a leading indicator that would give early warning, and explain the time gap between them.

Five minutes with a CEO is a test of editing, not of how much you know — and the pyramid principle is the tool that saves you. The principle inverts the instinct to build up to your conclusion: you lead with the answer first ('Sales are up 12%, driven mainly by the West region's new accounts'), then support it with a few grouped key reasons, then offer detail only if asked. Executives think top-down and will interrupt; if you bury the headline at the end of a chronological data tour, you will run out of time before reaching the point. So: conclusion, then the three reasons behind it, then evidence on demand. Structure a 5-minute sales-results briefing for me using the pyramid principle, and tell me what you would cut first if the CEO gave you only two minutes.

Twenty charts on one page is a classic symptom of an analyst showing their work instead of delivering an answer — and the problems are real. It overwhelms the viewer (no clear place to look first), it implies every chart is equally important (so none is), it slows the report to load, and it usually means the page has no single question it is trying to answer. The redesign starts not with charts but with a question: what decision does this page support? Then you lead with the one headline number or chart that answers it, group the genuinely supporting visuals beneath it, push detail to drillthroughs or secondary pages, and delete anything that does not earn its place. Walk me through how you would cut that 20-chart page down, and tell me the first question you would ask the stakeholder before redesigning.

**The HEART framework (Google's UX metrics):**

- Engagement: depth of usage (sessions, features used)

- Airbnb: Nights booked
- Spotify: Time spent listening
- Slack: Messages sent within a team

**Data storytelling structure (Barbara Minto's Pyramid):**
1. Situation: what is the context?
2. Complication: what has changed or is the problem?
3. Resolution: what should we do?
Present the resolution first (executive summary), then the supporting data.

**Dashboard critique framework:**
For every dashboard you review, ask:
- What decision does this dashboard enable?
- Who is the audience?
- What is the primary metric?
- What action should the viewer take if the metric is red?
common_mistakes: Tracking activity metrics instead of outcome metrics — 'number of emails sent' is an activity. 'Revenue per email' is an outcome. Track what matters.
No benchmark or target on dashboards — a number without context is meaningless. Always show target, last period, or industry benchmark alongside the metric.
Presenting data without a recommendation — a BI analyst who says 'sales are down 10%' without saying 'and here is what I think we should do' is only doing half the job.
Using charts without titles that state the insight — a chart titled 'Sales by Region' tells you nothing. 'West Region Leads in Sales but Has Lowest Margin' tells you the story.
Overwhelming the audience with precision — 12.3456% is not more useful than 12.3%. Match precision to the decision being made.

mastery_questions: groupby().agg() and pivot_table() in pandas both summarise data, but they shape the output differently, and choosing the right one saves you a reshaping headache. groupby().agg() collapses rows into groups and returns a long, tidy result — one row per group, columns for your aggregations — which is ideal when you are feeding the result into more code or a chart. pivot_table() reshapes into a spreadsheet-style grid, spreading one variable across the columns — closer to what you would build in Excel, ideal for a human-readable cross-tab (sales by region down the side, by year across the top). pivot_table also handles aggregation and missing combinations gracefully. So: groupby for tidy, code-friendly summaries; pivot_table for grid-shaped, presentation-friendly cross-tabs. Give me one analysis where pivot_table is clearly the better choice and one where groupby().agg() is, and explain the difference in the shape you get back.

merge() is pandas' join, and the 'how' parameter decides which rows survive when the two tables do not perfectly line up — getting it wrong silently drops or invents data. An inner join keeps only keys present in both tables (matched rows only — use it when you want strictly the overlap). A left join keeps every row from the left table and fills NaN where the right has no match (use it when the left is your master list you must not lose, like all customers even those with no orders). A right join is the mirror image. An outer join keeps everything from both, NaN-filling all gaps (use it to find what does not match on either side). The dangerous default assumption is that every key matches — it rarely does. Give me a use case for each of the four, and tell me which join would silently lose customers who never placed an order.

Missing values force a decision, and the wrong reflex — always dropping or always filling — corrupts analyses in opposite ways. You drop rows when the missingness is rare and random enough that losing them will not bias the result, and the row is unusable without the value. You fill (impute) when dropping would throw away too much data or bias it — filling with a mean, median, a forward-fill for time series, or a sensible default — but you must remember that imputing invents data and can flatten real variation. You flag (add a 'was_missing' boolean) when the fact that a value was missing is itself informative — a blank income field might mean something. The core question is always why the data is missing before you decide. Give me one situation each where dropping, filling, and flagging is the right call, and the risk of choosing wrong.

Month-over-month growth in pandas is a great little exercise because it chains three ideas: aggregate, shift, and compare. First you group sales by month and sum them into a monthly series. Then the key move is .shift(1), which slides the series down by one row so each month sits next to the previous month's value. Finally growth is (this_month minus last_month) divided by last_month, times 100 for a percentage — or more compactly, monthly.pct_change() times 100, which does the shift-and-divide for you. The insight beginners miss is that .shift() is what lets a row 'see' the row before it. Write me the pandas code in two steps — resample or groupby to monthly totals, then compute the percentage growth — and tell me what value the first month gets and why.

apply(), map(), and applymap() all run a function over pandas data, but each operates on a different shape, and using the wrong one throws an error or runs needlessly slowly. map() works element-wise on a single Series — use it to transform one column, like mapping region codes to full names. apply() is the flexible one: on a Series it works element-wise, but on a DataFrame it runs a function over each entire row or column (axis=0 or 1) — use it when your calculation needs several columns at once, like combining price and quantity. applymap() runs element-wise across every cell of an entire DataFrame — use it for a blanket formatting transform on all cells. So: map for one column, apply for row/column-level logic, applymap for whole-frame element-wise. Give me one concrete task suited to each, and explain why you could not just use apply() for all three.
