mastery_questions: Looker Studio and Looker share a name and a parent (Google) but are very different products, and knowing why both exist tells you when to reach for each. Looker Studio (the old Data Studio) is the free, self-serve dashboarding tool — you connect a source, drag charts onto a canvas, share a link; great for fast reports and small teams. Looker (the enterprise platform Google acquired) is a heavyweight modelling layer built on LookML, where data teams define metrics once, centrally and governed, so the whole organisation queries consistent, trusted definitions — it is about governance and a single source of truth at scale. Google kept both because they serve opposite ends: ad-hoc and free versus governed and enterprise. Tell me which one a five-person startup reaches for versus a thousand-person company that needs everyone to agree on what 'revenue' means, and why.

BigQuery's pricing flips a habit every analyst learned on traditional databases: it charges by the bytes your query scans, not by how many queries you run or how long they take. That single fact rewrites how you write SQL. SELECT * across a huge table is now actively expensive because it reads every column's bytes, so you select only the columns you need. Filtering on a partitioned column lets BigQuery skip whole chunks of data unscanned, slashing cost. And running an exploratory query repeatedly without limiting it can quietly burn real money. The mindset shift is from 'make it fast' to 'make it touch as few bytes as possible'. Give me two concrete changes to how you write a query under bytes-scanned pricing, and explain why SELECT * is a cost mistake rather than just a style one.

A Looker Studio calculated field is a new field you define with a formula on top of your connected data — the rough equivalent of a DAX measure in Power BI, but it is important to see how it differs. A calculated field is computed at query time over the rows the report is pulling, using Looker Studio's own function syntax, and it is scoped to that data source or chart. A DAX measure, by contrast, lives inside a modelled semantic layer with the full power of filter context and time intelligence, and is reusable across the whole model. So calculated fields are lighter and more local; DAX measures are richer and model-aware. Give me an example of a calculated field you would build in Looker Studio, and explain one thing a DAX measure can do that a Looker Studio calculated field cannot easily.

Partitioned and clustered tables are BigQuery's two main levers for cutting the bytes a query scans — and since you pay by bytes scanned, they directly cut cost. Partitioning splits a table into segments by a column, usually a date, so a query filtered to 'last 7 days' physically reads only those 7 daily partitions instead of the whole history — the rest is never touched. Clustering then sorts the data within each partition by other columns you often filter on (say, region), so BigQuery can skip blocks that cannot contain your filter's values. Together they mean a well-targeted query reads a tiny slice of a massive table. Explain why partitioning by date helps a date-filtered query so dramatically, and what clustering adds on top once you are already partitioned.

Data blending in Looker Studio combines data from multiple sources at the report layer — you join, say, a Google Ads source and a Sheets source on a common key right inside the dashboard, without touching the underlying databases. It is convenient when the data lives in different systems you cannot easily join upstream, or when you just need a quick combined view. But the trade-off matters: blending happens at query time in the report, with limits on join types and performance, whereas joining in BigQuery happens once in a governed, optimised query that the whole organisation can reuse and trust. So blend for quick, cross-source reporting; join in BigQuery when the combined data is core, large, or shared. Tell me a situation where blending is the right call, and one where you would push the join down into BigQuery instead, and why.

mastery_questions: The honest answer to 'what should AI do in BI' is: AI is excellent at the mechanical and the first-draft, and weak at judgment and context. Well-suited tasks: drafting a DAX or SQL query from a plain-English description (you still verify it), explaining an unfamiliar function or error, and generating boilerplate like documentation or repetitive transformations — work where the answer is checkable and the cost of a wrong draft is low. Tasks that need human judgment: deciding which metric actually matters to the business, interpreting whether a result is meaningful or an artifact of bad data, and any call where being confidently wrong has real consequences. The pattern: AI accelerates the typing; you own the thinking. Give me three BI tasks you would happily delegate to AI and three you would never, and explain the line that separates them.

When AI hands you a DAX measure using DATEADD() for 'sales growth vs last year', the dangerous move is to trust it because it looks plausible — confident-but-wrong is exactly the AI failure mode. Verification is not optional; it is the job. First, check the logic: DATEADD requires a proper, contiguous Date table marked as a date table, so confirm that exists or the function silently misbehaves. Second, test it against a known answer — pick a month where you can hand-calculate last-year sales and confirm the measure returns it. Third, probe the edges: what does it return for the first year (no prior year to compare), and does it handle partial periods correctly? AI gives you a hypothesis; data gives you the truth. Walk me through exactly how you would prove that DATEADD measure is correct before shipping it, and the specific case most likely to expose a bug.

Running AI-generated SQL against a production database without review is one of the fastest ways to cause a real incident, and the risks stack up. Correctness: the AI may misunderstand your schema and silently return wrong numbers that a stakeholder then acts on — a subtle JOIN that double-counts is worse than an obvious error. Cost and performance: an unoptimised generated query can scan enormous amounts of data, lock tables, or hammer a database that is also serving live users. And the catastrophic case: a generated statement that is not a harmless SELECT — an UPDATE or DELETE slipped in — could mutate production data. The rule is that AI output is a draft to be read, run first against a safe copy, and checked, never piped straight at production. Explain the three categories of risk, and the single guardrail that prevents the worst one.

Getting useful DAX out of an AI is a skill, and it comes down to giving it the context it cannot guess. A vague prompt like 'write a sales growth measure' yields generic, often-wrong code because the model does not know your model. A strong prompt includes: your table and column names exactly as they are (Sales[Amount], not 'the sales field'), the structure of your model (that you have a separate Date table, what the relationships are), the precise definition of what you want ('year-over-year growth as a percentage, comparing to the same month last year'), and any edge-case handling you need. The more of your real schema and intent you supply, the less the AI has to invent. Tell me the specific pieces of information you must include in a prompt to get correct DAX, and what typically goes wrong when you leave the model structure out.

The 'AI as co-pilot' workflow means the AI sits beside you accelerating the work while you stay in the pilot's seat making the decisions — not on autopilot. In practice: you decide the question and what would count as a real answer; the AI drafts the query, the transformation, or the first explanation; you read it critically, run it against real or sample data, and verify it; you interpret what the result means in business context; and you own the recommendation that goes to a stakeholder. What the AI cannot do is care whether the answer is true, understand the political and business stakes of being wrong, or notice when the data itself is lying. Describe the co-pilot loop step by step, and name the specific responsibilities that must stay with the human no matter how good the AI gets.

A BI portfolio is your proof of work. Anyone can list Power BI and SQL on a CV — very few people can show a dashboard, explain the design decisions, and walk through the DAX or SQL behind it. Those people get the interviews.

Your BI portfolio should demonstrate three things: technical skills (can you build a complete, well-structured Power BI report or SQL pipeline?), analytical thinking (can you find interesting insights and explain why they matter?), and communication (can you present data in a way that drives decisions?).

This week you package everything you have built into a portfolio, prepare for common interview question types (technical SQL/DAX questions, case study analysis, stakeholder communication scenarios), and practise until the answers are fluent.

mastery_questions: Walking an interviewer through your most complex DAX measure is really a test of whether you understand your own work or just got it to run. Pick a genuinely non-trivial measure — say a year-over-year growth percentage, or a rank-within-category, or a dynamic measure switched by a slicer — and structure your answer in three beats. First, what it calculates in business terms ('this shows each product's sales growth versus the same month last year'). Second, why the key functions are there — why CALCULATE was needed to override or set the filter context, why you used a VAR to capture a value before the context shifted. Third, how you tested it — the known month you hand-checked, the edge case (first year, blank periods) you confirmed. The interviewer is listening for whether you can explain the filter-context reasoning, not recite syntax. Pick a real measure and give me that three-part walkthrough now.

A 48-hour take-home dashboard is graded as much on process as on the final pixels, so resist the urge to start dragging charts immediately. The process that impresses: first, understand the question and the audience — what decision should this dashboard support, and who reads it? Second, profile the raw data — row counts, grain, data-quality issues, what each column means — before modelling anything. Third, build a clean model (a star schema with a proper Date table) rather than reporting off a flat mess. Fourth, write the three or four core measures that answer the question. Fifth, design the report top-down — headline answer first, supporting detail beneath, and ruthless removal of anything that does not earn its place. Sixth, leave time to document your assumptions and known limitations. Walk me through your 48 hours from raw file to finished report, and tell me what you would do first before opening Power BI.

This is a window-function and ratio exercise rolled into one, so let's reason it through. For each region you need total sales, total profit, profit margin (profit divided by sales as a percentage), and a rank by that margin. The first three come from a GROUP BY region with SUM aggregations and the margin computed as SUM(profit) / SUM(sales) * 100 — being careful to divide the summed values, not sum a row-level ratio. The rank then needs a window function over the aggregated result: RANK() OVER (ORDER BY profit_margin DESC), which ranks regions by their margin without collapsing them further. The subtle trap is computing margin correctly (aggregate then divide) and ranking on the aggregate. Write me that query, and tell me why computing margin as the average of per-row margins would give a different, wrong answer.

'5% to 6% is a 1% increase' is a confidently wrong statement, and how you correct it tells an interviewer whether you understand metrics or just numbers. The error is confusing percentage points with relative percentage change. Going from 5% to 6% is a one-percentage-point rise, but as a relative change it is a 20% increase (1 divided by 5). Those two framings can support wildly different stories, and choosing the flattering one to mislead — or stumbling into it by accident — is exactly what stakeholders do. Your job is to state both clearly: 'conversion rose one percentage point, which is a 20% relative improvement', so nobody is misled in either direction. Explain the difference between a percentage point and a percent change using these numbers, and tell me which framing you would lead with for an executive and why.

Discovering that a report you built has been wrong for three months is a character test, and the wrong instinct — quietly fix it and hope nobody noticed — is the one that ends careers. The right sequence is integrity-first. Immediately assess the impact: what decisions were made on the bad numbers, how wrong were they, and who relied on them. Then disclose promptly and clearly to the stakeholders affected — owning it fast builds far more trust than a cover-up that surfaces later. Fix the root cause, not just the symptom, and document what went wrong. Finally, add a control — a validation check or a reconciliation against a source of truth — so the same class of error cannot silently recur. Walk me through what you would do in the first hour and the first day, and explain why transparency protects you more than silence.

weeks.title: Capstone Project — Week 1: Design and Build
weeks.context:
The capstone is a complete, end-to-end BI project using a real dataset of your choice. Not Superstore — you have been building with that for 15 weeks. This week you choose a domain you care about (sports, finance, health, your own business data, public government data), source the data, design the data model, and build the first version of the report.

The deliverable is not a finished dashboard — it is a working prototype with a clear analytical question at its centre. Good BI projects start with a question: "What drives customer churn?", "Which products are dragging down overall margin?", "Where in the funnel are we losing users?" Every visual in the report should answer part of that question.

This week is design-heavy. Before you open Power BI, you sketch the report layout on paper or in Figma, define your measures, and verify your data model is correct. Skipping the design phase produces dashboards that look like they were assembled by someone clicking around — because they were.

mastery_questions: Every good capstone starts with a question, not a dataset — because a dashboard that does not answer a clear question is just decoration. So the first thing I want from you is the single analytical question your capstone exists to answer, phrased so that a specific person could make a specific decision from it ('which product categories are quietly losing margin, so we know where to renegotiate supplier costs?'). Then define how you will know it succeeded: what does the finished report let someone conclude or do that they could not before? A vague aim ('explore the sales data') produces a vague dashboard; a sharp question produces a focused one. State your capstone's core question for me, name the decision it informs, and tell me the concrete signal that would mean the report actually answered it.

Describing your data model is how you prove you built on rock, not sand — so walk me through it deliberately. Name your fact table (the events you are measuring — sales rows, sessions, transactions) and state its grain in one sentence: what does exactly one row represent? Getting the grain explicit is the foundation everything else rests on. Then name your dimension tables (the descriptive lookups that filter and slice the facts — Date, Product, Customer, Region) and how each connects to the fact. The thing I am listening for is whether your model is a clean star — facts in the middle, dimensions around it, a proper Date table — rather than a flat sheet. Tell me your fact table, its grain in one sentence, and your dimension tables, and explain why you chose that grain.

Writing the DAX for your three most important measures before you build the visuals forces you to think in business logic instead of dragging fields and hoping. Identify the three measures that actually carry your capstone's answer — not every number, the load-bearing ones (perhaps total revenue, profit margin, and year-over-year growth). For each, write the DAX out and be ready to defend it: which function does the real work, does it need CALCULATE to set context, does it depend on your Date table? Writing them first also surfaces model problems early — if a measure is awkward to express, your model is probably wrong. Give me your three core measures with their DAX, and for one of them explain the filter-context reasoning behind why it is written that way.

Designing for your audience is the difference between a report that gets used and one that gets ignored, and it comes down to deliberate inclusion and exclusion. Start by naming who opens this — an executive who wants the answer in five seconds, an analyst who wants to explore, an operator who needs one daily number? That answer dictates everything: an executive view leads with a single headline and hides detail behind drillthroughs; an analyst view exposes slicers and granularity. Just as important is what you left out — every chart you excluded because it did not serve that reader is a design decision worth defending. Tell me who your capstone is for, one thing you deliberately included for them, and one thing you deliberately left out, and why each choice serves that specific reader.

Naming your biggest data-quality issue up front is a sign of maturity — junior analysts hide problems, senior ones surface and handle them. Every real dataset has them: missing values, duplicate rows, inconsistent categories ('West' vs 'west' vs 'W'), wrong data types, or records that violate the grain. Identify the single worst one in your capstone data, explain how you detected it, and — crucially — how you are handling it and what bias your handling introduces (dropping rows? imputing? flagging?). Then state the honest impact: how does this issue limit what your analysis can claim? A report that quietly ignores its data quality is one wrong decision waiting to happen. Tell me your biggest data-quality issue, how you are handling it, and how it constrains the confidence of your conclusions.

common_mistakes: Starting with the visuals instead of the question — if you don't know what question you're answering, every visual decision is arbitrary.
Choosing a dataset that is too clean — real data has nulls, duplicates, type mismatches, and inconsistent naming. Cleaning it is part of the project.

Trying to include everything — scope down. A focused report that answers one question well is better than a sprawling report that answers nothing clearly.
weeks.debug_help:
**Data cleaning issues in Power Query:**
```
- Inconsistent date formats: Transform → Date → Parse
- Duplicate rows: Home → Remove Duplicates
- Null handling: Replace Values → replace null with 0 or 'Unknown'
- Text case inconsistency: Transform → Format → UPPERCASE / Capitalize Each Word
- Extra spaces: Transform → Format → Trim
```

**Relationship not working as expected?**
- Open Model view and verify cardinality (1:*, *:1, 1:1)
- Check that the join key has no duplicates on the 'one' side
- Check data types match exactly (whole number vs text)

**Measure returning blank instead of 0?**
```dax
-- Wrap with COALESCE or IF
Total Sales = COALESCE(SUM(Orders[Sales]), 0)
-- Or use + 0
Total Sales = SUM(Orders[Sales]) + 0
```

weeks.title: Capstone Project — Week 2: Complete and Present
weeks.context:
The capstone is complete this week. You finish building, polish the report, and deliver a presentation. The presentation is the most important part — a BI report that nobody understands is a failed report regardless of how good the DAX is.

Your presentation has two audiences: a technical peer (who wants to know about the data model, measures, and data quality decisions) and a business stakeholder (who wants to know the answer to the analytical question and what action to take). Practise both.

The other deliverable this week is a written retrospective: what worked, what you would do differently, and what skills you want to develop next. A BI analyst who can reflect honestly on their own work and identify gaps grows faster than one who treats every project as complete.

mastery_questions: The most important insight from your capstone is the one sentence a stakeholder would remember a week later — and being able to state it, with honest confidence, is the whole point of the project. So give it to me sharply: not 'sales vary by region' but 'the West region's margin is being silently eroded by discounting, and it is the single biggest drag on company profit'. Then do the thing that separates an analyst from a chart-maker: tell me how confident you are and why. What is the strength of the evidence, and just as importantly, what would invalidate it — a data-quality issue, a confounding variable, too small a sample, a correlation you have not proven causal? State your single most important insight, your confidence level, and the specific finding or error that would overturn it.

Walking through your data model end-to-end is the moment an interviewer decides whether you actually understand dimensional modelling. Go in order: name the fact table and state its grain in one sentence (what one row is), then each dimension table and what it describes, then the relationships — which tables join to which, on what keys, and in which direction filters flow. Mention the grain of each table explicitly, because mismatched grains are where models quietly break. What I am listening for is a clean star with a proper Date table and sensible one-to-many relationships, explained in terms of why, not just what. Walk me through your fact table and its grain, your dimensions and theirs, and the relationships between them — and flag any modelling compromise you made and why.

Cataloguing the data-quality issues you found and how you handled each is what makes your conclusions trustworthy rather than naive. Go through them honestly: missing values (did you drop, impute, or flag — and what bias did that introduce?), duplicates (how did you detect and resolve them without losing real records?), inconsistent categories or types you had to standardise, and any records that violated your grain. For each, state not just the fix but the impact on validity — imputing a quarter of your revenue figures means your totals are partly estimated, and you should say so. The mark of maturity is connecting each data issue to a specific limitation on what your analysis can claim. List the issues you found, how you handled each, and for the worst one, exactly how it constrains the confidence of your final answer.

'What would you build next?' reveals whether you see your capstone as finished or as a first version — and the strong answer shows you know its limits. Name the most valuable thing the report does not yet answer: a question a stakeholder would naturally ask next that your current model or data cannot address ('it tells us margin is falling, but not whether it is driven by discounting or rising costs — I would bring in cost-of-goods data to separate them'). Good 'next steps' are not 'add more charts'; they are the logical next question your analysis provokes, plus what data or modelling it would require. Tell me the single most valuable thing you would build with another week, the question it answers, and what you would need to do it.

A stakeholder challenging your finding is not an attack to defend against reflexively — it is a test of whether you are anchored to the truth or to your own work, and the right posture is intellectual honesty. First, take it seriously and ask exactly what they are questioning — the data, the method, or the interpretation. Then defend what is defensible with evidence: show the query, the sample size, the validation you did. But — and this is the part that earns respect — if their challenge surfaces something you missed (a data issue, a confounder, a better interpretation), you update your analysis rather than dig in. Being right matters more than being seen to be right. Walk me through how you would respond to a stakeholder who disputes your headline finding, and tell me the signal that would make you change your conclusion versus defend it.

**Report polish checklist:**
```markdown
## Pre-Presentation Checklist

### Data Quality
- [ ] All nulls handled with explicit decisions (filled, dropped, flagged)
- [ ] Date column correctly typed and marked as Date table
- [ ] Relationships verified (no inadvertent many-to-many)
- [ ] All measures spot-checked against source data for 3 known values

### Report Design
- [ ] Every page has a clear title stating its purpose
- [ ] Every visual has an axis label, legend, and title
- [ ] Colour palette is consistent and accessible (test with colour blindness simulator)
- [ ] No more than 5-6 visuals per page
- [ ] Primary metric is the largest or most prominent element on the page

### Performance
- [ ] Report loads in under 5 seconds (Import mode)
- [ ] No unnecessary columns imported (remove unused columns in Power Query)
- [ ] Calculated columns moved to measures where possible

### Accessibility
- [ ] Alt text added to all visuals (Format → General → Alt text)
- [ ] No information conveyed only by colour
```

**Presentation structure (10 minutes):**
1. Context (1 min): what question are you answering and for whom?
2. Data overview (1 min): what data did you use and what were the key quality issues?
3. Key findings (5 min): walk through 3-5 insights, one page at a time
4. Recommendation (2 min): based on the data, what should the audience do?
5. Q&A (1 min): demo the interactivity
common_mistakes: Presenting data without a narrative — don't click through charts. Tell a story: 'we started by looking at X, which revealed Y, which led us to investigate Z'.
Demoing a live report without testing it first — always demo with the report pre-loaded in the Service, not loading in Desktop during the presentation.
Not handling challenges gracefully — 'that's a great question, I'll investigate and follow up' is a professional answer. Making up data to fill a gap is not.
Skipping the recommendation — every BI presentation should end with a clear 'so, here is what I recommend'. Without it, the data just sits there.
Not archiving the project — store the .pbix, data source files, and all SQL/Python code in a git repository. You will reference this project in interviews for years.
